evidence.text: The page identifies this as a modern vector redraw of 干 in Shuowen seal-script style, based on the s01611 image in hanziyuan.net data. The vector was uploaded in 2007 and released to the public domain; attribution is appreciated but not required. This is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact image.

evidence.text: The page identifies this as a modern vector redraw of 干 in oracle-script style, sourced to character databases including Sinica and hanziyuan. The page classifies the image as a public-domain representation of ancient script, with attribution appreciated but not required. It gives no specific artifact, inscription, or date for the pictured form and marks the file as needing a time period; do not treat it as a securely dated Shang artifact glyph.
evidence.title: File:干-oracle.svg — Wikimedia Commons

evidence.text: The article identifies the mid-Western Zhou 豦簋 inscription as the earliest securely identifiable 干 in its account. It describes that form as a round shield-like body with a forked top. Later Western Zhou forms regularize the top to a short horizontal stroke, a form continued in later scripts. The attribution of proposed earlier Shang forms remains a scholarly proposal.

evidence.field: oracle-bone and bronze forms; competing interpretation
evidence.text: The database interprets oracle-bone and bronze 干 as a decorated shield and reports Xu Zhongshu’s alternative that some oracle-bone forms related to 單 depict a forked hunting implement. This is a report of competing paleographic interpretations; the database page itself is not an independently inspected artifact image.

search_audit.query: site:commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File: "干-seal.svg"; site:commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File: "Shuowen Seal Radical 047.svg"; 干 seal script Shuowen Commons image file; 干 Western Zhou bronze 豦簋 graphic history shield paleography
search_audit.outcome: Search returned both exact Commons file pages and a paleographic article. Opened the 干-seal page and inspected its description, source, and public-domain terms; opened the oracle-style file through the Commons page’s listed alternatives and inspected its description, period limitation, source, and public-domain terms. The exact Shuowen Seal Radical 047 page returned a cache miss on open; search-result text exposed its CC BY-SA 3.0 description, but its direct image could not be inspected, so it was not selected. The NTU CASE page supports the secure mid-Western Zhou 豦簋 attestation and later graphic changes.

search_audit.query: 干 shield pictograph oracle script image Commons file; 干 豦簋 Western Zhou bronze glyph paleography
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the Commons oracle-style redraw page and CUHK paleographic entry. Commons’ listed bronze-style filename could not be opened (cache miss), so no bronze image candidate was selected. CUHK reports shield interpretation and competing analysis; the NTU article supplies the period and graphic-history context.

gaps: The selected oracle-style Commons vector does not identify a particular artifact or securely date the depicted form; the source page itself marks its period as needing verification. Its use should be limited to an undated modern redraw of an oracle-style form, alongside the separately cited paleographic account.

The page for Shuowen Seal Radical 047.svg was not accessible for direct inspection, and its original pixels were not inspected. It is therefore excluded despite the page appearing in search results with a CC BY-SA 3.0 notice.

No exact, accessible Commons page establishing and licensing a particular 干 bronze glyph was confirmed in this pass; the suitable seal-style redraw and the qualified oracle-style redraw are the selected candidates.

limitations.text: The oracle-style drawing is not tied on its Commons page to a particular dated inscription, and the file page flags its period as needing verification. Treat it as a modern redraw, not direct evidence that the shape was used in a securely identified Shang inscription.
The chosen drawings are modern redraws. For the secure dating and later form changes, rely on the separately cited paleographic account rather than treating these images as artifact photographs.
